title: Ready, SETT, Go: SETT Execs Drill Down on the Spanish Sovereign Venture Capital Fund That Will Drive Industry Conversation at San Sebastián
description: One of the major industry narratives at this year’s San Sebastián Festival, running Sept. 18-26, will be the presentation of SETT, the venture capit
body: One of the major industry narratives at this year’s San Sebastián Festival, running Sept. 18-26, will be the presentation of SETT, the venture capital fund of Spain’s Ministry for Digital Transformation.SETT director general Javier Ponce and its audiovisual director María Coronado deliver a practical guide to Spain’s governmental investment drive powering up companies in Spain: What it’s doing, why, and where it could go in the future. The companies it s investing in – with more to be revealed – are likely to be among the most dynamic in Spain.What, explained very briefly, are the objectives of SETT’s Spain Audiovisual Hub strategy?Javier Ponce: SETT is a public investment entity that manages investments in strategic, transformative sectors, including the audiovisual industry. It serves as a public catalyst for growth, employment, innovation and talent—all core elements of the audiovisual sector. SETT has managed the Spain Audiovisual Hub Fund, an instrument established under Spain’s Recovery Plan and financed through the European Union’s Next Generation funds.Through the Spain Audiovisual Hub Plan, SETT provides financing and equity or quasi-equity investments, either directly to companies in the sector or through financial intermediaries active in the audiovisual industry. The objective has been to attract private investment and improve access to finance for projects related to films, television, animation, multimedia and interactive content, among others. Priority has been given to high-impact projects focused on creating audiovisual content and intellectual property rights while ensuring that those rights remain with the production companies.And the rationale of a sovereign venture capital fund’s co-investment model?Ponce: It is based on public-private collaboration to launch transformative initiatives that, because of their innovative nature, involve additional risks that make it difficult to attract purely private funding. Only highly liquid, large-scale markets with a long-established audiovisual industry are able to mobilize sufficient capital to finance major new productions or transformative industry initiatives.SETT’s Spain AVS Hub fund could draw down up to €1.5 billion ($1.75 billion) from NextGeneration E.U. funding. According to María Gonzalez Veracruz, investments made are just under €250 million. Her explanation is that you simply ran out of time. Could you comment?Ponce: Indeed, European funds have been fundamental for Spain, and the Recovery Plan has played a key role in driving major structural reforms and stimulating economic growth. However, it is also true that these funds came with specific requirements, including strict implementation deadlines, which made optimal execution more challenging.For the audiovisual sector, the possibility of co-investing alongside a public entity represented a major innovation. Time therefore became a critical factor, as market participants first needed to understand the role and implications of partnering with a public investor that shared both risks and returns.The next challenge is to ensure that these investments continue to thrive, identify new opportunities, and maintain confidence in the talent and ambition of Spanish audiovisual companies, which now benefit from SETT’s backing.SETT, however, is not over, I believe. Obviously it has to exercise governance over investment accords now struck. I believe as well that there are plans to launch a new program España Crece, with a €13.3 billion ($15.6 billion) budget, held by ICO, but whose investments will be handled in part by SETT, if I understand correctly. Could you comment?Ponce: The audiovisual sector will remain one of SETT’s strategic areas of activity and will continue under new fund “España Crece”. We have begun discussions with ICO to define the procedures and framework for collaboration between the two institutions, ensuring the continuation of co-investment in strategic technologies and sectors.SETT has represented a significant shift in the way public investment in strategic industries is conceived. Through SETT, the State acts as a catalyst and partner in the most innovative areas of the economy, with the objective of positioning Spain at the forefront of transformative industries. That is why we invested in the audiovisual sector and why we will continue to do so.Its ability to generate industrial activity, employment and broad economic impact makes it a strategic sector that will continue to enjoy our support.Could you illustrate the rationale of SETT’s co-investment model in one or two of the investments made and the obvious benefits it could bring to the companies Spain’s film-TV industry.Coronado: The SETT model has been built on three pillars. First, it adopts an industry-wide approach, rather than a project-based one, addressing the entire audiovisual business ecosystem. Second, its investment facilities are directed at the equity capital of companies or regulated investment vehicles. Third, it promotes public-private partnership instruments on a medium-long term.Under this model, promoters must convince a genuinely private investor that their company represents a worthwhile investment opportunity. SETT co-invests alongside the private investor on a pari passu basis: public investment is intended to support companies, but always under the same terms and conditions as private capital.This approach strengthens both domestic and international private investment in companies based in Spain, while also attracting foreign businesses that see Spain as an attractive location to establish their operations. Clear examples include the South African transactions involving The Refinery and Moonlighting, with a combined investment of €25 million, as well as Amuse Labs and Milo, two leading examples of Spain’s animation industry, which have mobilised €13 million and €19 million respectively.My sense is that SETT investors can indeed help companies scale, create more such expertise and build infrastructure. But would you agree?Coronado: In my view, the main challenge for the coming years is to consolidate the model we have been promoting and supporting. It is essential to continue strengthening and diversifying support policies so that Spain can establish itself as a global hub for the audiovisual industry over the long term. This means supporting every segment of the industry according to its specific needs.Scale is undoubtedly part of the challenge, as is ensuring the availability of the infrastructure needed to accommodate medium- and large-scale productions, strengthening technical training, and fostering talent across the industry. It will also be important to continue enhancing the tax framework and the legal and regulatory environment to maintain Spain’s competitiveness, while further developing public-private investment instruments.In addition, it will be essential to understand the cash-flow financing needs of projects to address the full range of companies’ financing requirements. Finally, the industry’s ability to adapt and diversify will remain critical, both in terms of technology and creativity, as well as business models and corporate structures.In your view, does the introduction of sovereign venture capital in the Spanish film and TV industry encourage a change of mindset in the industry?Coronado: Yes, absolutely. It creates new opportunities. It is essential to think in terms of medium- and long-term business strategy, rather than focusing only on immediate projects. It enables companies to strengthen their capital base, making them more ambitious, better able to protect their intellectual property, diversify, expand internationally, and bring their products to market more effectively.What have you learnt in the two years of the Spain AVS Hub Phase II which you would like to apply in future investments by SETT under España Crece?Coronado: The main learning here is the confirmation that SETT has a clear and necessary purpose for the industry, both in attracting private investment and foreign companies, and in creating opportunities for the local industry. It is important to allow more time for business plans to mature and for companies to secure private investment.Can you outline very briefly what the SETT event at San Sebastián Festival will consist of?Coronado: As you would expect, we will have a strong presence at the festival, with a wide range of activities. On Sept. 20, the Secretary of State for Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence, through the Ministry for Digital Transformation and the Civil Service, which is leading the Government’s Spain Audiovisual Hub Plan, will host an event in which SETT will present the huge progress we have made in financing the audiovisual sector and new ongoing projects. Additionally, on 22 September, I will take part in a panel discussion at the conference organised by the CAA as part of Spanish Screenings Investment & Tech. That same day, we will also host an exclusive roundtable with investment funds and banks specialising in the audiovisual sector, bringing together both international and Spanish participants. We also have a few more surprises in store, which we will unveil throughout this very important festival for the industry.

schema.headline: Ready, SETT, Go: SETT Execs Drill Down on the Spanish Sovereign Venture Capital Fund That Will Drive Industry Conversation at San Sebastián

title: ‘Ride or Die’ Canceled by Prime Video After One Season
description:
“Ride or Die” has been canceled by Prime Video after one season, Variety can confirm.

	The streamer’s Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer-led bud
body:
“Ride or Die” has been canceled by Prime Video after one season, Variety can confirm.

	The streamer’s Hannah Waddingham and Octavia Spencer-led buddy dramedy premiered in July of this year. It was first reported that Spencer and Waddingham were teaming up for the series in December 2023.

	Per the show’s official logline, “‘Ride or Die’ follows best friends Debbie Claybourne (Spencer) and Judith Burton (Waddingham) who thought they knew everything about each other, except Judith turns out to be an international assassin. When a mysterious figure emerges from Judith’s past and a hit goes horribly wrong, both of their worlds are turned upside down as they’re forced to go on the run together. It’s a race against time and a road trip across Europe, with law enforcement, highly trained assassins, and some very dangerous criminals at their heels.”
	

	In her review of Season 1, Variety’s Aramide Tinubu wrote that “‘Ride or Die’ works best when it fully leans into the ‘Thelma & Louise’ aspects of the central storyline… Spencer and Waddingham have a robust and genuine chemistry — a companionship that will undoubtedly resonate with countless viewers. Moreover, watching Waddingham as a full-fledged action star is something everyone should be witnessing on a daily basis.”

	Other cast members included Ed Skrein, Calam Lynch, Savannah Steyn, Jamie Parker, and Jacky Ido, with Sylvia Hoeks and Bill Nighy.

	Tessa Coates created the series and serves as executive producer and showrunner along with Matt Miller and director Peyton Reed. The show is produced by Paramount Television Studios, Amazon MGM Studios as well as Andy and Barbara Muschietti’s Double Dream and Octavia Spencer’s Orit Entertainment. Coates, Miller, and Reed executive produce alongside Spencer for Orit Entertainment; Waddingham; Andy Muschietti, Barbara Muschietti, and Irene Yeung for Double Dream; Brian Clisham; and Stephanie Kluft.

schema.headline: ‘Ride or Die’ Canceled by Prime Video After One Season

title: Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta ‘Don’t You Dare’ Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: ‘Do Not Cave’
description: Mark Ruffalo is encouraging California attorney general Rob Bonta and his coalition of 11 other state AGs not to settle their lawsuit against Paramo
body:
Mark Ruffalo is encouraging California attorney general Rob Bonta and his coalition of 11 other state AGs not to settle their lawsuit against Paramount Skydance and keep David Ellison from acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery.

	“Don’t you dare, [Rob Bonta], do not cave,” Ruffalo wrote on X. “5,670 filmmakers put their necks on the line for you to fight this merger. Another 75,000+ and counting have signed to tell you not to concede in just 3 weeks. You work for the people — the very people who will be hurt if you let this lousy deal filled with empty promises go forward. Please sign to send a message to the AGs and Paramount. Reject the deal. The people don’t want it!”
	

	Ruffalo is one of Hollywood’s most outspoken stars about opposing the merger. He recently found himself in a back-and-forth with Paramount, in which a studio rep called him “antisemitic” for calling out the Ellisons’ connection with Israel.


	Paramount Skydance’s $111 billion deal for Warner Bros. was approved by the Department of Justice in June. However, the deal was put on hold thanks to the antitrust lawsuit from Bonta and his team of state AGs. The Wall Street Journal, citing anonymous sources, reported Friday that Paramount Skydance and Bonta are in “advanced talks” to reach a settlement.

	Ruffalo isn’t the only one asking Bonta to hold his ground. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts wrote on Facebook Saturday morning that President Donald Trump banning CNN from the White House is a warning of things to come if Paramount Skydance swallows Warner Bros. (Trump also banned MSNOW and Politico).
	

	“As Trump tries to ban CNN from the White House, it would be a massive mistake to cave on the Paramount merger,” Warren wrote. “The last thing we need is another Trump-controlled media conglomerate abusing its power to stomp out competition. This is a dangerous merger.”

schema.headline: Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta ‘Don’t You Dare’ Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: ‘Do Not Cave’

title: Ruby Rose Remembers ‘Best Friend’ Hayden Panettiere: ‘All That She Ever Wanted Was to Have Her Story Told’
description:
Ruby Rose got emotional when asked about her friend, Hayden Panettiere, who died Aug. 16 at 36.

	Rose told Entertainment Tonight that Panettiere wa
body:
Ruby Rose got emotional when asked about her friend, Hayden Panettiere, who died Aug. 16 at 36.

	Rose told Entertainment Tonight that Panettiere was her “best friend” and that they “spoke every day for five years.”

	“I didn’t even think we were going to be friends,” Rose said, tearing up. “I didn’t know if I wanted to have any celebrity friends, because I didn’t have a great experience with the industry.”


	She shared how the two of them first met, saying, “I saw her, she saw me, and I just remember thinking, ‘Oh, no.’ And then she ran up anyway and was like, ‘Hey, I’m Hayden. Can we go talk somewhere? We’ve got a lot in common.’ I just laughed.”
	

	The two quickly became close after realizing they “had everything in common,” Rose said. Throughout their five-year friendship, they texted each other every day to check in. 

	“Hayden, all that she ever wanted was to have her story told her way, on her terms,” Rose said.

	Panettiere, who was known for her roles on “Heroes,” “Nashville,” “Scream 4” and “Scream VI,” openly spoke about her struggles with drug and alcohol addiction in her 2026 memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning.” Days after her death, the Drug Enforcement Administration joined the investigation, working with South Carolina’s Greenville Police Department to determine her cause of death.

	Hollywood stars shared tributes online after news of her death became public, including Jack Coleman, who played her father on “Heroes.”

	“I’m heartbroken. I couldn’t begin to put my thoughts into words until now, and they will be inadequate,” Coleman wrote. “I’ve loved Hayden since day one of the pilot of ‘Heroes,’ 20 years ago, when she introduced herself by shouting ‘daddy’ and throwing her arms around me. From that day on, she called me daddio. She was Haydini, because she was a magician.”

schema.headline: Ruby Rose Remembers ‘Best Friend’ Hayden Panettiere: ‘All That She Ever Wanted Was to Have Her Story Told’

title: ‘Sweet Magnolias’ Creator Reacts to Netflix Cancellation: ‘I Hope Serenity Will Always Have a Place in Your Heart’
description: Following the news that “Sweet Magnolias” has been canceled at Netflix, creator and showrunner Sheryl J. Anderson is looking back on the romantic dr
body:
Following the news that “Sweet Magnolias” has been canceled at Netflix, creator and showrunner Sheryl J. Anderson is looking back on the romantic drama’s 5 Season run.

	“Living in Serenity for five seasons has been a privilege and a blessing,” Anderson shared in the caption of an Instagram post Saturday. “The people I’ve met and worked with — our incredible writers, cast, crew, executives, and producers — have touched my heart and changed my life.”
	

	She continued: “And our fans have been amazing in their passion for our characters. Thank you all. Though our journey has sadly come to an end, I hope Serenity will always have a place in your heart. Keep pouring it out!”


	The Netflix show first premiered on the platform in May 2020, and starred JoAnna Garcia Swisher, Brooke Elliott and Heather Headley. Originally adapted from the book series by New York Times best-selling author Sherryl Woods, the streamer announced that the show continuously ranked among Netflix’s Global Top 10 in over 60 countries after announcing its return for a fifth season in 2025.

	The “comfort drama,” as described by Netflix, followed the lifelong friendship between Maddie (Swisher), Dana Sue (Elliott), and Helen (Headley) “as they juggle relationships, family and careers in the charming small town of Serenity, S.C.”

	Though “Sweet Magnolias” may be coming to an end, Netflix announced that Swisher and Anderson would be teaming for a new drama series titled “Ladies of the House.”

	Variety previously reported that Anderson will serve as showrunner, with Swisher potentially starring and executive producing with Kate Gordon under their Rolling Clover banner, alongside executive producers at Black Label Media.
	

	The logline reads, “When the charismatic owner of a winery dies unexpectedly, his wife and two adult daughters must battle through their issues with each other in order to confront challenges with the business, their extended family, and the men in their lives. Good friends and good wine will aid in the journey to hang on to the winery, but what matters most is that they find a way to hang on to each other.”

schema.headline: ‘Sweet Magnolias’ Creator Reacts to Netflix Cancellation: ‘I Hope Serenity Will Always Have a Place in Your Heart’

title: Protestors March Outside Ed Sheeran Concert After Macklemore Was Dropped From Tour: ‘It’s Not Going to Stop Until Palestine is Free’
description: Pro-Palestinian protesters gathered outside Ed Sheeran’s concert at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday night as the singer returned
body:
Pro-Palestinian protesters gathered outside Ed Sheeran’s concert at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday night as the singer returned to the stage for the first time since Macklemore was dropped from his Loop Tour following his onstage remarks in support of Palestine.

	For attendee Jodi Rhoden, an organizer at Writers Against the War in Gaza, the protest represents something “much bigger than us.” “It’s much bigger than Ed Sheeran. It’s much bigger than Macklemore. It’s a movement for Palestinian lives, and it’s not going to stop until Palestine is free.”
	

	Rhoden also noted that while there are many people who have “lost their livelihoods for speaking the truth about this genocide,” she feels the “tide is turning”: “You can see that with the way that Ed Sheeran fans are reacting, and the way that people are rallying behind that for more. It seems like we’ve really hit a tipping point, and public opinion has changed.”


	Grace, an 18-year-old college student, said it was important for her to attend the protest “because we have to continue talking about Palestine.” Going into the evening, she is hoping that Sheeran “acknowledges what he did was wrong and says he wants to free Palestine.”

	The demonstration, which drew a crowd of around 100 participants, was planned for 4:30 p.m. outside the South Philadelphia stadium, ahead of Sheeran’s 8 p.m. performance. Organizers said speakers from Writers Against the War on Gaza, the Boycott Cooknsolo Coalition and Shut Down Day & Zimmermann were expected to participate. The Philly Palestine Coalition and Shut Down Day & Zimmermann had also circulated calls for supporters to demonstrate outside the venue.
	

	The protest comes amid mounting fallout from Macklemore’s removal from Sheeran’s U.S. stadium tour. The rapper had opened Sheeran’s Sept. 4 and Sept. 5 concerts at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where he performed his 2024 pro-Palestinian protest song “Hind’s Hall,” displayed footage from Gaza and called for a “Free Palestine” from the stage.

	Days later, tour promoter Messina Touring Group announced that Macklemore would no longer appear on the remaining dates. The promoter said several stadiums had indicated they would not permit concerts to proceed with Macklemore on the lineup and that keeping him on the bill could jeopardize the remainder of the tour.

	Macklemore subsequently said New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft played a central role in the decision. Kraft’s company owns Gillette Stadium, where Sheeran is scheduled to perform Sept. 25 and 26, and Macklemore alleged that Kraft rallied other stadium owners behind an ultimatum that the rapper be removed.

	Kraft acknowledged that he opposed Macklemore performing at Gillette Stadium, saying in a statement that his participation in the two concerts there “would cross that line.” Kraft argued that Macklemore’s presentation of the Israel-Hamas war ignored the actions of Hamas and contributed to divisiveness and hate. Macklemore has defended his advocacy for Palestinians and rejected accusations that it amounts to antisemitism.

	Sheeran, meanwhile, has said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by the tour promoter and venues rather than by him. The singer said he had spoken with venue owners, promoters and activists in an effort to reach a resolution but was unable to do so.

	The decision prompted a wider exodus from the Loop Tour. Finneas, Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Beoga — the Irish group that had been performing as part of Sheeran’s live band — all withdrew following Macklemore’s removal. Saturday’s Philadelphia show was consequently pushed from its originally advertised 5:30 p.m. start to 8 p.m., with Sheeran listed as the only act on the bill.

	The controversy has also prompted a local debate over the decision to exclude Macklemore from the publicly owned stadium. The Philadelphia chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations sent an open letter to the Philadelphia Eagles, the City of Philadelphia, Lincoln Financial Group and others criticizing the move and raising questions about free expression and advocacy for Palestinian rights. The organization also filed a public-records request seeking information about who told Messina Touring Group that Macklemore could no longer perform at the venue.
	

	Ahead of Saturday’s demonstration, Philadelphia police said they were coordinating with the venue and event organizers and would adjust staffing according to public-safety needs. A police spokesperson separately said officers had been in communication with Sheeran’s team over security arrangements for the concert.

schema.headline: Protestors March Outside Ed Sheeran Concert After Macklemore Was Dropped From Tour: ‘It’s Not Going to Stop Until Palestine is Free’

title: Ed Sheeran Addresses Macklemore Controversy While on Stage at First Concert Since Rapper Dropped From Tour: ‘What Is Happening in Gaza Is Catastrophic and Unjustifiable’
description: Ed Sheeran addressed the controversy surrounding Macklemore’s removal from his Loop Tour on Saturday night, speaking from the stage at Philadelphia’
body:
Ed Sheeran addressed the controversy surrounding Macklemore’s removal from his Loop Tour on Saturday night, speaking from the stage at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field during his first concert since the rapper was dropped from the trek.

	“Before I play some songs tonight, I hope it’s okay if I say a few words about this last week,” Sheeran said at the top of Saturday’s show. “I’m used to my music being criticized, and I’m always happy to take that because I’m lucky. A lot of you like my stuff, and to be honest, I’m surprised. I’m not surprised that I’ve even done it. You know, it’s normal. But this week, the criticism was about something much more important, and I’ve had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I’m so, so sorry.”
	

	Sheeran continued: “I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet. My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone, and that matters hugely to me. Honoring my commitment to my fans is also completely essential to who I am, and that is why I’m here tonight on my own and continuing my current tour.” 


Ed Sheeran addresses the controversy surrounding Macklemore’s removal from his tour and says, “What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable.”“Before I play some songs tonight, I hope it’s okay if I say a few words about this last week,” Sheeran said at the top of… pic.twitter.com/ZhtujolkKK— Variety (@Variety) September 20, 2026


	Later in the set, Sheeran introduced the musicians who replaced Beoga, the traditional Irish folk group that pulled out of his remaining U.S. tour dates. “There are certain songs that just don’t work on the loop pedal, so when my friends dropped out of the show, I was thinking, ‘How am I gonna keep the show the same, and how am I gonna get musicians to stand on stage with me in a week when no one wants to stand on stage with me?’”
	

	“I just wanna say before they come on stage [that] they said yes to being on stage with the knowledge that the world thought I was a certain type of person,” he continued. “They said yes with the knowledge that the world may hate them too for standing on stage with me and I am so grateful for them being on stage tonight and standing on stage with me in front of you guys.”

	The controversy also prompted Sheeran to scrap the B stage — a smaller secondary platform closer to the crowd where he typically performs several songs — because he “was scared of what might happen if [he] stood in the middle.”

	“I’m gonna be totally honest with you, I didn’t know what this audience would be like tonight,” he said on stage. “I didn’t know if I would have things thrown at me. I didn’t know if people would be angry at me.”

	Saturday’s concert marked Sheeran’s first performance since a tumultuous week for the U.S. leg of his Loop Tour, which saw Macklemore removed from the remaining dates following the rapper’s onstage remarks in support of Palestinians during Sheeran’s Sept. 4 and 5 shows at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

	During his MetLife performances, Macklemore spoke about the war in Gaza and the West Bank and told the stadium crowd, “Free Palestine.” His set also included “Hind’s Hall,” his 2024 protest song supporting Palestinians. The remarks drew criticism from some Jewish and pro-Israel organizations, including the Israeli-American Council, which called for Macklemore to be removed from the tour.

	Messina Touring Group, the promoter behind the U.S. leg of the Loop Tour, subsequently announced that Macklemore would no longer appear on the remaining dates. The company said venues had informed the promoter that they would not allow concerts featuring Macklemore to proceed, a situation it said could have resulted in cancellations affecting hundreds of thousands of ticket holders.

	While Sheeran addressed the decision in a statement earlier this week, stressing that Macklemore’s removal was made by the promoter and venues rather than by him, he again acknowledged that he is “deeply worried about the idea that venues pre-approve content for performance.” “This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world,” he said.
	

	At the time of his initial statement, Sheeran said he was “appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine,” describing the suffering caused by the war as a “human tragedy,” while explaining that he has generally sought to keep his concerts focused on “unity, joy, escapism, love” rather than his own political views. On Saturday, he restated these feelings, though also speaking more explicitly about where he stands on the Israel-Palestine conflict. 

	“I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division,” he said. “But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore. What happened in Israel and at the Nome Museum Festival on Oct. 7 was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable, and disproportionate. Our hearts can be broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians’ lives, children’s lives and the systemic injustice we’re seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked.”

	He continued, “I am already speaking to people across the spectrum to work out how to make a contribution that helps victims of these terrible times, and listening and learning because I do not know enough.”

	After Macklemore was dropped, he responded to his removal in a statement, saying that he and Sheeran had held “difficult conversations” in the aftermath of the MetLife shows. While expressing respect for Sheeran personally, the rapper challenged the singer’s preference for remaining publicly neutral and said he did not regret using the tour stage to speak in support of Palestinians. Macklemore has since said he will donate $1 million to Palestinian relief organizations.

	The fallout quickly spread beyond Macklemore. Singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe and Danish band Lukas Graham, who had been expected to support Sheeran on upcoming North American dates, both withdrew from the tour. Finneas, who was scheduled to join Sheeran for a run of South American dates later this year, also pulled out, while Beoga — longtime collaborators who had been performing as part of Sheeran’s live show — exited as well. All four cited Macklemore’s removal in announcing their decisions.
	

	The Philadelphia date nevertheless proceeded as scheduled Saturday at Lincoln Financial Field, kicking off the next stretch of Sheeran’s U.S. stadium run.

schema.headline: Ed Sheeran Addresses Macklemore Controversy While on Stage at First Concert Since Rapper Dropped From Tour: ‘What Is Happening in Gaza Is Catastrophic and Unjustifiable’

title: Henry Winkler Says His Name Was Cut From ‘Scream’ Poster Because ‘You Were the Fonz’ and It Would ‘Knock the Balance of Horror Off’
description:
Finding out his name wouldn’t be used on the “Scream” poster wasn’t one of Henry Winkler’s happier days.

	The “Happy Days” star played Principal Ar
body:
Finding out his name wouldn’t be used on the “Scream” poster wasn’t one of Henry Winkler’s happier days.

	The “Happy Days” star played Principal Arthur Himbry in the original “Scream” film, which went on to become one of the most successful horror franchises. But despite his character’s entrance receiving applause during screen tests for the 1996 movie, Winkler revealed the studio refused to put his name on the poster.
	

	“The studio comes to me and says, ‘We can’t put your name on the film. We cannot put you anywhere near the poster,’” Winkler said in an interview for “In Depth With Graham Besinger.” When he asked why, the studio said, “Well, you were the Fonz, and you will knock the balance of horror off if we let them know you’re in it.”


	Although it left him feeling “insulted,” the actor didn’t overtly protest the studio’s decision. 

	“I said, ‘OK. What can I do?’ I went home upset,” the actor said. “I was bewildered a little bit.”

	He later learned the same people who had informed him his name wouldn’t be used on the poster were also the ones who asked him if he would do press for the film’s release. Winkler ultimately agreed, noting he obliged for himself, director Wes Craven and the movie as a whole.

	Now, looking back 30 years later, Winkler said the experience taught him to navigate the unknown.

	“That’s the lesson. You just show up,” he said, also pointing out that “you have no idea what’s going to happen, but that’s out of your control.”

	“Scream” also starred Neve Campbell, Courteney Cox, David Arquette, Drew Barrymore and Matthew Lillard. The franchise’s latest film, “Scream 7,” became the highest-grossing installment with $176.9 million.

schema.headline: Henry Winkler Says His Name Was Cut From ‘Scream’ Poster Because ‘You Were the Fonz’ and It Would ‘Knock the Balance of Horror Off’

title: Pete Davidson and Colin Jost Were Clowned for Buying the Staten Island Ferry. They Just Proved Everyone Wrong.
description:
“There’s an epidemic affecting our nation’s young people. The epidemic is fear.”

	As I scrolled through Instagram on my ride downtown to the Snappl
body:
“There’s an epidemic affecting our nation’s young people. The epidemic is fear.”

	As I scrolled through Instagram on my ride downtown to the Snapple Island Ferry Comedy Show, a reel from The Free Press popped up. Professor Arthur Brooks was making the case that “Gen Z is perhaps the most risk-averse generation in history.”

	Now, I’m no psychologist. I’m a social media editor. And I theorize that some of that fear Brooks describes comes from our overexposure to a digital world that, seemingly, has all the answers. And when someone makes a decision outside the purview of algorithmic logic — like buying an abandoned ferry for $280,000 at a city auction — they are at the mercy of, well, being completely clowned.
	

	That’s exactly what the news cycle did to Pete Davidson and Colin Jost after they joined a group of investors to buy the decommissioned John F. Kennedy in 2022. Built in 1965, the JFK was the oldest ferry in the Staten Island fleet when it was retired last August due to mechanical failures. Davidson and Jost intended to transform the vessel into a floating entertainment venue.“Davidson, who’s no longer with SNL, might need to call his agent to book those gigs — turning the 57-year-old ship into a nightspot is likely to cost millions,” The New York Daily News reported. The headline read: “Retired NY Ferry Bought by Pete Davidson and Colin Jost Is Full of Asbestos, Roaches, Say Ex-Crew Members.”

	The social media hate laid on thick, too: “Have you heard of the hottest club in the city?” one person tweeted (per the LA Times). “It’s called ‘Tetanus’ and it’s located in the rusted belly of a decommissioned Staten Island Ferry. You’ll dance the night away while also always being just moments away from drowning.”

	Years had passed without hearing about the ferry until I got an unexpected email in my inbox: “EMBARGOED: Invite to NYC’s Most Unexpected Comedy Club From Pete Davidson and Colin Jost.”
	

	As it turned out, the “SNL” comedians partnered with Snapple to give New Yorkers an “unexpectedly refreshing break from the daily grind,” transforming their vessel into the Snapple Staten Island Ferry for a free, one-night-only floating comedy show.

	Could the comedians have listed tickets for $200 a pop and still packed the ferry? Undoubtedly. Instead, they dropped a limited batch of free tickets at 3 p.m. each day (Sept. 3-8). The resulting buzz and scramble among young New Yorkers to secure tickets (not totally unlike the IMAX 70mm frenzy surrounding “The Odyssey”) was much more valuable than the low six figures a sold-out show might have grossed at the door.Those lucky enough to make it aboard became a test audience for two brand comebacks, each fiercely looking to win over a younger generation before betting on a much bigger, more calculated swing.

	The first is Snapple, which started phasing out its signature glass bottles in 2017, replacing them with plastic (the transition was complete by 2021). The company justified the brand’s “massive makeover” as a decision made “with the evolution of sustainability in mind.” The operational savings from slashing the cost of manufacturing a bottle to roughly a third of what it once was probably looked pretty savory to the big-wig execs at Keurig Dr Pepper. Consumers weren’t as quenched.



	

					Sean K Fitzpatrick
	



	Snapple eventually budged in the fall of 2025, launching a limited glass-bottle revival at select bodegas and retailers across New York, citing a “demand for nostalgia from an OVERWHELMING number of consumers.” The brand has yet to commit to a wider or permanent return, but it was clearly testing the waters with this major brand activation.

	Hosting Snapple’s revival party was Davidson and Jost’s own comeback project to replenish the New York comedy scene, taking the form of a floating, popsicle-orange vessel. They once played the purchase off as a joke on “SNL,” with Jost quipping, “We thought the whole thing through” (sarcasm implied). But four years later, this one-night-only comedy show offered them a real opportunity to float their idea.


	The main room was packed. Because the ferry, naturally, didn’t have one big corridor, an overflow room projected a live feed of the main stage (shaped like a blocky ‘T’).

	“You’re media, right?” an event coordinator asked me. “Yes!” I had zoned out. “Then we better put you up here.” She whisked me straight to the front and pointed at two young women, who immediately jolted to their feet and shuffled toward the far end of the bench running parallel to the stage.“I, uh, I’m sorry I took your seats,” I told the two women as I sidestepped past them. They glanced at each other and giggled. “It’s okay,” one of them said. “Trust me.”
	

	It took me a couple of minutes to figure out what she meant. Then I pulled out my phone to take a picture of the stage: a black barstool, a (glass!) Peach Tea Snapple and a mic stand. I wasn’t just in the front row. I was in the hot seat. The very hot seat, directly under the mic stand. Stage lights beamed down on me, and the ferry cabin itself was extremely muggy. (I guess in Davidson and Jost’s master plan, A/C hit the cutting room floor.)

	The room skewed younger millennials and older Gen Z. Most toward the front looked like (or probably were) influencers who’ll look good on camera. Usually, I’ll recognize at least a few media friends in a crowd like this. Not here. I tried making friendly banter with the dude sitting next to me. He was cordial, but his energy read: Nope.

	At nine o’clock sharp, the lights went dark. Davidson and Jost emerged from beneath the neon Snapple Island Ferry sign to rapturous applause. This would be the first and last time we’d see the two co-hosts all night.

	I’ve encountered Davidson and Jost in the wild before, but this tight vantage point popped any illusion of celebrity. Picture sitting in the front row of a movie theater.

	“This is something we’ve wanted to do for like five years, so thank you guys for coming out,” Davidson opened. “And thank you to our sponsor, Snapple.” After holding a beat for the applause, Davidson exclaimed, “The glass is back, baby!”

	Jost added: “I also feel like we should acknowledge our former sponsor: my accountant’s suicide note.” He smirked. “Snapple asked me to say this.”

	They then turned to the first of three lingering storylines from the news cycle they clearly wanted to address. First, the aforementioned clowning.“The amount of shit that people have talked,” Davidson said. “Well, suck it!”

	“Everyone feeling hot and nauseous? That’s a good feeling,” Jost asked the crowd before moving on to news topic numero dos. “Obviously we’ll get going soon. We’re gonna stop at the Strait of Hormuz.” But when Jost looked over at Davidson to tee up the next punchline, it became clear the geopolitical reference sailed right over his head.

	“I like how you thought I would know what that is,” Davidson quipped back. He glanced down at the shot clock. 8:17 remaining. The sweat was palpable.

	“I love that this is our body language,” Davidson said, leaning into their candid awkwardness as he and Jost stood marooned on opposite ends of the oversized T-shaped stage. “It’s truly like we’re waiting for someone to start a fight.”
	

	Laughing along with the crowd, Jost admitted, “We don’t know exactly what to do.” The audience roared. That unvarnished honesty, the willingness to take themselves down a notch, clearly resonated with the audience of young people accustomed to spending hours each day swiping through content engineered to mask imperfection.

	“We have an incredible show. There are so many great comedians here,” Jost said. “Macklemore is here tonight.” The crowd erupted. Jost stalled on a few uhs, his eyes scanning the room as he debated whether it was worth taking the joke any further.

	Davidson took advantage of the moment. “You wanted to make a stance tonight, right?” he poked. “Colin was talking mad shit backstage, dude. He was like, ‘Macklemore doesn’t have shit on what I’m about to say.’”

	Red in the face, Jost quickly rowed back to safer waters. “So, in other news…” From there, the remainder of their opener centered on Davidson’s recent concussion. But the lineup of fierce rising comics (with considerably less to lose) didn’t shy away from the insecurities and taboos their Gen Z audience might be too anxious to confront.

	Matt Richards, who served as emcee for the night (effectively filling the role many of us presumed Davidson and Jost would play), set the tone for the night by chugging an entire Snapple in one go and then telling a story of how he tried to suck his own penis as a teenager. “Happy to say it didn’t work out,” Richards said. “If it did, I wouldn’t be here.” In an alternate timeline, he’d “live under a bridge and suck my own dick all day.”

	As the crowd observed Richards, he gauged their reactions, taking the temperature of how far he could push them. The other comics were about to dive into some risqué material — he was just warming them up.

	Richards wiped a bulk of sweat from his forehead. The humidity was becoming hard to ignore. Playfully, he advised Davidson and Jost to sort out the A/C situation before the next show. That’s what I was thinking.


	When Chris Rock sat down with Variety’s Selome Hailu for his first in-depth interview since “The Slap,” he recalled “dying a death” during a stand-up set in Oakland in ’96. He was workshopping his controversial “Black People Versus N—s” bit, which would eventually appear in his landmark HBO special “Bring the Pain” that helped catapult Rock into rock-star comic status.

	“People wanted to fight because I didn’t have it right yet,” Rock explained in his cover story interview. “You gotta go over the line to find the line. That’s what people don’t understand. When a comedian gets in trouble for saying something at the club, it’s like, ‘Dude, that’s what the club’s for.’”

	Overcoming the fear of vulnerability, on both sides of the stage, is what makes the club special. A physical vessel where smartphones, despite the event’s plea for ample social coverage, were repeatedly told to stay tucked away.
	

	At one point, a Staten Island photographer named Sean lowered his camera to snap a portrait on his phone of “Impractical Jokers” star Sal Vulcano mid-set. Vulcano immediately stopped. “No cellphones, sir,” he said. “It’s right up in my face.” Sean held up his DSLR, cutting Vulcano’s budding rant short.

	“This guy’s just like- oh, you work here?” Vulcano said, his tone instantly changing. “Okay, you’re not fired. You’re great. I love you.”

	Even an Impractical Joker, after hundreds of public challenges and punishments designed to push the limits of embarrassment, could still tense up when a cellphone camera caught him experimenting with a new bit. “That was the ending,” he told the crowd after telling a story about buying health insurance for his newborn. “I thought that would get a bigger laugh.”

	The crowd loved it. He was hyper-fixated on grading his performance.

	Perhaps that’s why crowd work is so effective. Is there any other setting better designed to experience a flash of public humiliation?“I like this guy,” Richards said, pointing at me. “You look like a Disney villain.”

	“Gaston!” He belted out a Disney song. 

	Caitlin Peluffo stormed the stage with material in the — let’s call it — advanced workshopping stages. After boldly announcing to the crowd that she was “dropping eggs,” she turned to ask if I knew what ovulating was.

	I responded with a sarcastic “Ehh!” and bobbed my head. “Go figure,” she said. “I wouldn’t expect anything less from a man wearing khakis.”

	After another minute or two of hyper-sexual jokes, she circled back to me.

	“Do you like pussy?”
	

	The camera whipped in my direction.

	I froze. Then hit her with the same ambiguous emote.

	Why did I just do that? I literally-

	“You’re really wishy-washy on the answer, sir.”

	“You gotta leave a little mystery.”

	“Leave a little mystery?”

	Gulp.

	“Those pants aren’t leaving any mystery, I’ll tell you that,” she fired back. “You’re not circumcised, I can tell.” The crowd woo-ed. “That’s okay. I like me a full-body boy,” she continued. “I’m not an easy cum. You better crack your knuckles.”

	I cracked my knuckles on both hands. She smiled. Peluffo got what she needed from me. Mercifully, she moved on to her next victim.

	“Are you a tough cum or an easy cum?” she asked an attractive, reserved young woman. “Which one are you?” I had never seen a face more red in my entire life. “ANSWER THE FUCKING QUESTION!”

	“I’m easy!” she finally blurted out.

	“Fuck!” Peluffo shot back. “You’re probably cumming right now.”


	On the way out, ferry workers dressed in sailor uniforms were handing departing guests free Snapple. I grabbed a glass peach tea and popped a squat on the pier. It really does taste better.

	As I sat there taking in the night, the sound of clinking glass got louder and louder. Sure enough, I spotted a small procession bolting away from the boat with entire cases of Snapple.

	I walked over and asked a few of the workers why they were giving them away. A woman with a dyed-blonde bob leaned toward me, lowering her voice.

	“Please, take one now and leave before anyone sees you,” she said. “We need to get rid of all of these before the end of the night.”



	

					Sean K Fitzpatrick

President Trump
                          I Will Create an A.I. Force!!!
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            First there was Space Force ... now, President Donald Trump has announced that in order to monitor artificial intelligence, he will create -- you guessed it -- an A.I. Force.
      
    
            The prez took to Truth Social Saturday morning to claim that the growing concern about the nefarious capabilities of A.I. are simply part of a hoax ... this despite several members of the tech community direly sounding the alarm and sharing instances of A.I. going rogue.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He wrote ... "We will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth of this incredible industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!"
      

            Having said that, Trump wrote that he'd be looking out for "BAD" instances of the technology acting out.
      
    
            The president added ... "For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar.'"
      
    
            In the last two weeks, there's been a slew of disturbing revelations about the technology ... and some of what's gone down is downright eerie.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The U.S. military reportedly almost started a war with China based on a faulty intelligence report generated by A.I. ... and OpenAI just shared their discovery of 6 "unexpected or concerning" new incidents.
      
    
            Time will tell if Trump can get his A.I. Force to lift off in time ... before A.I. goes too far.
